title: How to Understand the New Age of War
gist: In a Foreign Affairs podcast, war historian Lawrence Freedman argues that the U.S.-Iran war is a 'stupid war' built on the short-war fallacy and muddled objectives, leaving Hormuz leverage with Tehran's hardliners, while Ukraine remains a hurting stalemate with a ceasefire hard to negotiate. He downplays Russian nuclear use, warns of Indo-Pacific proliferation as U.S. guarantees weaken, and says AI and drones diffuse too fast to confer lasting advantage, so mass matters more than exquisite quality.

insights.claim: The U.S. war with Iran was a 'stupid war' because its main consequences, closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a resurgence of Hezbollah, were widely forecast by anyone who had studied Iran.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: The Hormuz disruption was a predictable, structural outcome rather than a surprise, so energy risk premia tied to it are likely to persist.
insights.quote: it is a stupid war because the consequences were forecast
insights.locator: I mean, it is a stupid war

insights.claim: The decision to go to war with Iran followed a plan brought by Benjamin Netanyahu, with no full discussion even inside a hollowed-out Trump administration, unlike the year of debate before the Iraq war.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Reduced deliberative capacity in Washington raises the odds of abrupt, poorly hedged military decisions and policy shocks.
insights.locator: And I think what to me still is what’s staggering

insights.claim: U.S. objectives in the Iran war kept shifting, from regime change to a better nuclear deal to reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and the war has left no nuclear deal at all and an Iranian regime reminded why it might want nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Nuclear proliferation risk from Iran has risen, extending the horizon of Middle East risk premia.
insights.quote: So you’ve got no nuclear deal at all at the moment and an Iranian regime that has been reminded of why it might want nuclear weapons.
insights.locator: And I think the problem with Iran is the political objectives were muddled

insights.claim: Decapitation strikes do not make regimes like Iran's collapse, and the idea of killing the right leaders to strike a Venezuela-type deal was a fantasy.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Do not bet on regime change in Tehran as a path to normalized Iranian oil flows.
insights.locator: I mean, the Israelis seem to have convinced themselves

insights.claim: Iran moved on the Strait of Hormuz far faster than expected, unlike its cautious response in June 2025; the U.S. had concluded Iran would not fight hard, while Iran concluded it needed to and prepared.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Past restraint is a poor guide to future Iranian behavior; energy markets should not underwrite Iranian caution.
insights.locator: And then I think what surprised people was the speed

insights.claim: Iran became fixated on the Strait of Hormuz as leverage and passed up an MoU that would have unfrozen assets and let its oil industry flourish, even though it has shown it can close the strait at any time.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Hormuz remains a reusable lever even after reopening, so shipping and oil risk premia should not fully normalize on any deal.
insights.quote: they’ve shown that they can close it at any time
insights.locator: Now, all of that was made possible by the MoU

insights.claim: Iranian hardliners have used the war to take control, and the United States has used up much of its capacity, able to hit tankers bound for Iranian ports but not to materially change Iranian capabilities, so it relies on economic pressure.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: A military resolution is unlikely near term; watch sanctions and tanker interdictions as the main levers affecting oil flows.
insights.locator: Now we’ve got a real problem

insights.claim: Iran may be waiting until after the U.S. midterm elections before moving, seeking to punish Trump much as it held the hostages until Reagan's inauguration in 1980-81.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Expect Hormuz-related disruption to persist at least through the November 2026 midterms; a pre-election deal is less likely.
insights.locator: In my mind, but maybe this is too influenced

insights.claim: The Iran war's economic consequences are pretty serious and its legacy will persist for many years.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Treat the Iran-war energy shock as a multi-year macro factor rather than a transitory spike.
insights.locator: These are pretty standard mistakes

insights.claim: Iran's war has exposed the United States as an unhelpful ally in the Gulf, creating a war in which regional allies such as Saudi Arabia were hurt without much U.S. help.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Gulf states may hedge away from U.S. security dependence, with implications for arms purchases and OPEC-plus alignment.
insights.quote: the US doesn’t turn out to be a very helpful ally
insights.locator: All you can see in the Gulf now

insights.claim: Military planners systematically plan for short wars because protracted war would require far greater mobilization, stockpiles and resources, which is why leaders repeatedly start wars expecting quick victory.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: When wars start, markets should assume longer duration than officials promise; defense stockpile and munitions demand tends to surprise upward.
insights.quote: nobody in their right mind plans to launch a long war
insights.locator: I think the problem is that’s what military planners plan for

insights.claim: Russia has had to transform its economy for the worse because its planned short war in Ukraine failed.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: War economies degrade long-run growth; Russian economic weakness is structural.
insights.locator: And indeed, if you try to think about how to prepare for a protracted war

insights.claim: The Pentagon under Pete Hegseth judged the Iran war by military objectives rather than political ones, and his claims of victory at the ceasefire now look embarrassing.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Discount official victory claims; political outcomes, not battlefield metrics, drive the durability of ceasefires and risk premia.
insights.locator: And I think there was also a mindset

insights.claim: Putin cannot win the war in Ukraine because Russia cannot occupy and subjugate all of Ukraine, and even the Donbas has been ruined as a prize, yet he persists because failure would undermine his credibility.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Expect a prolonged war with no decisive Russian victory; Russian economic degradation continues.
insights.quote: this is a war Putin can’t win
insights.locator: So I think one of the first things I wrote

insights.claim: Both Ukraine and Russia expect another six-month period in which the key questions are whether Ukraine can survive the winter and find more money to fund the war, primarily from Europe.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: European fiscal commitments to Ukraine over winter 2026-27 are a key catalyst for the war's trajectory and for European defense budgets.
insights.locator: I think, at the moment, the general view

insights.claim: Russian forces have suffered real setbacks, for example around Lyman, while Ukraine is bringing new ballistic missiles on stream and showing originality in tactics and technologies.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Ukraine's domestic weapons production is a growing factor; watch Ukrainian defense-tech and European co-production.
insights.locator: And we’ve seen recently in Lyman

insights.claim: Even a simple ceasefire in Ukraine would be extremely hard to negotiate because the sides disagree on where the front line is, Russia will demand sanctions relief, and the U.S. cannot deliver sanctions relief without the EU, UK and Canada.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of ceasefire headlines; sanctions relief for Russia requires multilateral agreement and is a long way off.
insights.quote: even just getting a ceasefire agreement in place could be really difficult
insights.locator: So I don’t think a ceasefire would be very easy

insights.claim: American mediation efforts on Ukraine are amateurish, though they remain available if Putin decides he wants a deal.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Peace depends on Kremlin decision-making, not U.S. mediation quality; don't trade on U.S. envoy activity.
insights.quote: the American mediation efforts are pretty amateurish
insights.locator: I mean, the American mediation efforts

insights.claim: Russia's system does not give Putin the truth about the war, and the prevalence of personalist leaders such as Putin, Trump, Erdogan, Netanyahu and Xi makes international outcomes hard to predict with historical models.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Geopolitical risk is increasingly leader-specific; scenario analysis should center on individual decision-makers.
insights.quote: in the end, when you’ve got these types of individuals in leadership positions, predictability becomes very difficult
insights.locator: Well, I mean, you’re talking about individual psychologies

insights.claim: Russian hybrid attacks in Europe, including explosives, cyberattacks and drone incursions, are aimed at eroding European support for Ukraine, and Putin may be counting on different governments in France, Germany and the UK.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: European election outcomes are material to Ukraine support; hybrid threats support European defense and security spending.
insights.locator: Yeah, and it’s a worry

insights.claim: Russian nuclear use in Ukraine is unlikely because the arsenal is what makes Russia a great power and using it offers no obvious gain, while repeated threats by Medvedev and figures like Karaganov have lost credibility.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Nuclear-escalation scares tied to Ukraine are likely overpriced tail risks; Western red lines have been overly cautious.
insights.quote: I don’t particularly think it’s high on Putin’s to-do list
insights.locator: I’d be more sanguine on that

insights.claim: Nuclear deterrence broadly works: NATO has not joined the Ukraine war, Russia has not attacked NATO territory, and India-Pakistan clashes have been contained, though containment gets harder each time.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Direct NATO-Russia war remains a low-probability scenario; India-Pakistan escalation risk is rising at the margin.
insights.locator: I mean, it seems to me there’s two things

insights.claim: Doubts about U.S. security guarantees could push allies toward their own nuclear weapons, a bigger problem in the Indo-Pacific than in Europe, and Japan or South Korea could build them fairly quickly.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Proliferation in Northeast Asia would reshape regional risk premia and defense spending; watch debate in Tokyo and Seoul.
insights.quote: the small print seems rather large at the moment
insights.locator: The other thing that’s going on is what happens to countries

insights.claim: In Europe, the UK and France are working out how to frame their nuclear capabilities to reinforce wider European security as reliance on the U.S. declines.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Supports the European strategic-autonomy and defense-spending theme.
insights.locator: In Europe, you’ve got the UK and France

insights.claim: AI already speeds targeting and swarm management, but it will not eliminate the fog of war because AI will be fighting AI and rarely gives one side a decisive advantage.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Be wary of defense-AI narratives promising decisive edges; value accrues to scale and adoption rather than monopoly.
insights.quote: basically AI is going to be fighting AI
insights.locator: In terms of targeting, AI already makes a difference

insights.claim: Military technologies diffuse quickly: drones pioneered in Ukraine and earlier Syria are now used widely, including in Sudan, and smartphones give everyone GPS, satellite imagery and instant communication once reserved for militaries.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Cheap, commoditized drone and dual-use tech benefits volume manufacturers and erodes Western technology premiums.
insights.locator: So there’s a diffusion of these technologies

insights.claim: A central lesson of Ukraine and Iran is that the West focused too much on exquisite, high-quality equipment and forgot that mass and numbers still matter.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Favors high-volume munitions, drones and industrial capacity over boutique platforms in defense allocation.
insights.locator: I think the point that we’re left with after Iran

insights.claim: Precision weapons were wrongly assumed to mandate a cleaner style of warfare; the same technology that allows a military to avoid hospitals allows it to hit them.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Technology does not dictate how wars are fought; political objectives do.
insights.quote: The same technology that allows you to avoid hospitals allows you to hit hospitals
insights.locator: But I think the mistake we made

insights.claim: Defenses remain weaker against air threats than against land threats, echoing old debates about whether the bomber always gets through.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Sustained demand for air and missile defense is structural across theaters.
insights.locator: So this takes you back to familiar questions

themes.theme: China, Taiwan and U.S. force posture

insights.claim: China is unlikely to seek an early war over Taiwan because it has gained ground by being vaguely menacing and holding its positions, though it takes offense easily and quickly resorts to sanctions, as with Australia over COVID.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Base case is coercive economic pressure, not invasion; firms in countries that offend Beijing face sanction risk.
insights.locator: Yeah. So I think that the Chinese are set on a course

insights.claim: The U.S. alliance system in the Indo-Pacific is more complicated and tenuous than NATO, and after the Iran war the U.S. must decide what its vast military system is for.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: A U.S. posture review could shift procurement and basing priorities toward Asia after the Iran war.
insights.locator: So I think it’s just something that we’ll end up watching

insights.claim: Military power rarely delivers definitive results, and the tragedies of the past decade stem from a lack of skepticism about what force can achieve, especially in occupying and subjugating populations.
insights.speaker: Lawrence D. Freedman
insights.so_what: Discount promises of quick, decisive military outcomes; conflicts tend to become prolonged and costly.
insights.quote: The trouble with violence is it seems like it’s definitive, that it just sorts stuff out, and it rarely does.
insights.locator: My own view, maybe this is just a function
